notes.meaning: Asaph calls God's people to listen carefully to his teaching. The word for instruction refers to God's truth delivered by His messenger. To incline one's ear means to bend forward in humble, reverent attention to God's word.

The psalmist announces that he will teach using parables and lessons from the past. These dark sayings are not meant to confuse, but are deep truths from Israel's history that require thoughtful reflection. Jesus later used these very words to describe His own practice of teaching the crowds through parables.

These lessons are truths that God's people have heard, known, and received from earlier generations. True faith is anchored in real historical events that godly ancestors carefully passed along. God's truth is not invented anew by each generation, but faithfully preserved and handed down.

Parents and leaders are commanded not to keep God's truth hidden from their children. Instead, they must tell the next generation about the Lord's praiseworthy acts, His mighty power, and the wonders He has performed. Passing on these stories helps young people learn to honor and worship God.

God established His law in Israel as a lasting witness of His covenant will. He commanded parents to teach these commands diligently so that future generations, including children not yet born, would grow up knowing them. In turn, those children would one day rise up and teach their own offspring, keeping the faith alive.

The true purpose of teaching God's story is so children will put their confidence in God alone. Remembering what God has done keeps people from forgetting Him and gives them strength to obey His commands. Real faith in God's goodness leads directly to faithful obedience in daily life.

Learning God's ways helps the next generation avoid repeating the mistakes of their ancestors. Israel's forefathers had been stubborn and rebellious, with hearts that were neither steady nor loyal to God. God calls every new generation to break the cycle of unbelief and remain true to Him.

The soldiers of Ephraim were skilled archers equipped for war, yet they retreated on the day of battle. Although they had weapons and military strength, their courage failed when testing came because their trust was not in God. Their physical retreat mirrored their spiritual failure to stand firm for the Lord.

The deeper reason for their defeat was that they broke God's covenant and refused to follow His law. They quickly forgot the miracles and mighty deeds the Lord had performed before their eyes. When people forget God's past mercies, their faith weakens and disobedience soon follows.

God performed astonishing miracles right before their ancestors in the land of Egypt, especially near the ancient city of Zoan. Zoan was a major royal district of Pharaoh where God sent the plagues to set His people free. God displayed His power in that prominent place so that His deliverance could never be denied.

The Lord parted the waters of the Red Sea so that His people could pass through safely on dry ground. He piled up the roaring waters upright like a solid wall on either side. This miraculous escape proved that even the forces of nature obey the command of the Creator.

God guided His people through the wilderness with a pillar of cloud during the day and a bright fire throughout the night. The cloud shaded them from the scorching desert sun, while the fire provided light and warmth in the darkness. Through these visible signs, God constantly reassured them of His loving presence and guidance.

When the people were parched in the desert, God split hard rocks at places like Rephidim and Kadesh to give them water. Instead of a small trickle, water poured out like great rivers and deep oceans to satisfy everyone. God demonstrated that He can easily supply refreshing life even in the driest wasteland.

Despite all these incredible miracles, the people continued to sin and rebel against the Most High in the wilderness. Their discontent only worsened, showing that God's goodness did not change their hard hearts. Complaining against God right where He was caring for them made their rebellion especially offensive.

The people deliberately tested God by demanding special food to satisfy their cravings. They were not merely asking for what they needed to survive, since God was already providing for them. Instead, they yielded to selfish appetite and demanded rich meat to suit their taste.

The people spoke boldly against God, asking insolently whether He was really able to prepare a feast in the wilderness. They admitted that He had cracked the rock to bring forth water, yet they doubted whether He could provide bread and meat. Their unbelief led them to question God's almighty power even after seeing His wonders with their own eyes.

When the Lord heard their insolent grumbling, His anger flared up against Israel like a raging fire. His wrath was stirred because they refused to believe Him or trust in His power to save and protect them. Unbelief deeply offends God because it treats His faithful promises as untrustworthy.

Even after they doubted Him, God commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven in mercy. He showered down manna all around their camp, providing grain straight from the sky so they would have plenty to eat. God met their stubborn complaints with abundant grace, feeding them daily from His heavenly storehouse.
